author: mindmap-write
readerQuestion: How much of my paycheck will I keep after federal income tax and payroll tax? [PAA unread - DataForSEO unavailable; ac 2/12 how-much and accuracy pattern: how much will i net on my paycheck, is paycheck calculator accurate]

presentation.placement: Page top, directly under the opening answer
presentation.reason: Take-home depends on pay, pay frequency, filing status and pre-tax retirement contributions, so the reader needs to enter them.
readerInputs: Filing status (single, married filing jointly, head of household)

interaction.reason: Adjustable inputs change the answer; a static table cannot cover each reader's pay, hours or filing status.

animation.reason: Static result cards answer faster; no sequence or change over time needs motion.

decisionGap: Readers see gross pay but not what survives federal income tax and payroll tax, and the site's bracket tool excludes payroll tax so it cannot answer take-home pay.
finding: A single filer at $60,000 pays $5,020 federal income tax, $3,720 Social Security and $870 Medicare, leaving $50,390 a year ($1,938.08 per biweekly check, 84.0% of gross) before state tax. Across $40,000 to $150,000 single, take-home share falls from 85.8% to 75.9%.
conditions: 2026 federal law, standard deduction, annual-liability estimate (not IRS Pub. 15-T withholding). Pre-tax retirement lowers income tax only; Social Security and Medicare apply to gross. Additional Medicare 0.9% modeled as employer withholding above $200,000 for all statuses. State and local tax, credits, health premiums, other pre-tax items, extra W-4 withholding, tips, overtime and senior or QBI deductions are not modeled.
whatWouldChange: State or local income tax, itemizing, credits, extra W-4 withholding, pre-tax premiums, or a change in 2026 IRS figures change the paycheck; married couples' final Additional Medicare liability uses the $250,000 MFJ threshold.
caseDecisions: Retrieved cases.json holds only unrelated Layer3Labs owned-property records (e.g. Drones & Defense); none overlaps a pay-conversion or take-home calculator, so no client or fleet record is used and none is claimed. No client-conversation attribution on this page.
method: taxable = gross - pretax - standard deduction; federal tax by 2026 brackets (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32); Social Security 6.2% up to $184,500; Medicare 1.45% plus 0.9% above $200,000 (IRS Topics 751 and 560); net = gross - pretax - federal - Social Security - Medicare.
units: USD per year and USD per paycheck (26 biweekly default); percent of gross
limitations: Annual-liability estimate with the standard deduction only; excludes state and local tax, credits, itemized deductions, Section 125 premiums, HSA, extra W-4 withholding, tips, overtime, senior and QBI deductions; filing status limited to single, married filing jointly, head of household.
counterexample: A state income tax or a W-4 with extra withholding makes the real check smaller than the estimate; pre-tax 401(k) of $10,000 on $100,000 cuts take-home by $7,800 rather than $10,000 because federal tax falls by $2,200 (modeled output pretax_100000_10000).

provenance.scopeAndLimits: Calculated from IRS 2026 figures for a W-2 employee on the standard deduction; annual-liability estimate; federal and payroll tax only.
provenance.publicMethod: On-page 'How Take-Home Pay Is Calculated' and '2026 Federal Figures Used' sections with IRS links and the exclusions list.
provenance.placement: howItWorks paragraph and the 'Take-Home Pay at Different Salaries' section

takeaway: Single filer at $60,000 keeps about $50,390 a year before state tax (84.0%). Applies to W-2 employees on the standard deduction; the answer changes with state tax, credits, extra withholding or premiums. Estimate, not withholding advice.
selectedMedium: interactive tool with the key answer, assumptions and finite tables readable in the static page
testingDecision: Ordinary format: calculated page; finance topic and calculator are outside _experience.md section G. No tested label, howWeTested or tested schema.
